results.title: How to Prevent Catastrophic Forgetting in ANNs
results.content: Catastrophic forgetting is a problem that affects artificial neural network (ANN) models when they learn new tasks and forget the previous ones. Catastrophic forgetting occurs when the weights of an ANN are updated to optimize a new task, but this interferes with the previous knowledge stored in the same weights. Catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks (ANNs) can be prevented through strategies like rehearsal, regularization, continual learning, and employing techniques like Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) or Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) to retain past knowledge while learning new tasks. To quantify the extent of catastrophic forgetting, researchers use different metrics that compare the performance of an ANN before and after learning a new task. Techniques such as replay, which involves exposing the model to old data, and regularization methods like Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) or synaptic intelligence (SI) can help retain previous knowledge while learning new tasks. Architectural modifications like modular networks or progressive neural networks also aid in reducing catastrophic forgetting by segregating knowledge or allocating specific resources for new tasks. Regularly updating the network on old tasks or employing lifelong learning approaches can help maintain a balance between old and new knowledge. Thankfully, several metrics can quantify the loss of past knowledge: Accuracy Drop: We compare the model's performance on the old task before and after learning the new task. Regularization methods prevent catastrophic forgetting in neural networks: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC): Penalizes significant changes in vital weights, protecting knowledge from previous tasks. Regularization methods like Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) or Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) can combat catastrophic forgetting in ANNs. These preserve important weights or gradients learned from previous tasks, minimizing interference when training on new data. Another way to prevent catastrophic forgetting is to use replay methods that rehearse the old knowledge while learning the new task. Use replay methods to expose the model to previous data during new task training: - Experience Replay: Maintain a replay buffer of samples from old tasks and periodically include them in the training set. A third way to prevent catastrophic forgetting is to use architecture methods that modify the structure of the ANN to accommodate the new task.

results.title: Catastrophic Forgetting: Understanding AI Memory Loss - ProjectPro
results.content: Catastrophic forgetting, or catastrophic interference, refers to the abrupt loss of previously learned information when new information is introduced, particularly in neural networks and artificial intelligence systems. Catastrophic forgetting occurs primarily in artificial neural networks when learning new information interferes with previously acquired knowledge. This adjustment can disrupt the weights that were previously fine-tuned for earlier learned data, causing the network to forget past knowledge. Without specific strategies to preserve important knowledge, neural networks can easily forget previous information when learning new data. These methods collectively help neural networks to continuously learn from new experiences without forgetting previously acquired knowledge, making them more robust and adaptable. Catastrophic forgetting is a critical issue in fine-tuning large language models, where new learning can overwrite and erase previously acquired knowledge. Catastrophic Forgetting is when a neural network forgets previously learned information upon learning new information, crucial in continual learning scenarios. In Linear Regression, Catastrophic Forgetting can lead to substantial loss of previously learned relationships between variables when new data is introduced, affecting model performance and reliability.

results.title: Neuromimetic metaplasticity for adaptive continual learning without catastrophic forgetting
results.content: Artificial neural networks are known to suffer from catastrophic forgetting: when learning multiple tasks sequentially, they perform well on the most recent task at the expense of previously learned tasks. Here we tested the hypothesis that implementing a sleep-like phase in artificial neural networks can protect old memories during new training and alleviate catastrophic forgetting. Here, using a model neural network of the hierarchical visual pathway of the brain, we show that invariance of object detection can emerge spontaneously in the complete absence of learning. While deep neural networks have surpassed human performance in multiple situations, they are prone to catastrophic forgetting: upon training a new task, they rapidly forget previously learned ones. Here, using an artificial deep neural network that models the ventral visual stream of the brain, we show that number-selective neurons can arise spontaneously, even in the complete absence of learning. In artificial neural networks, such memory replay can be implemented as ‘generative replay’, which can successfully – and surprisingly efficiently – prevent catastrophic forgetting on toy examples even in a class-incremental learning scenario. One challenge that faces artificial intelligence is the inability of deep neural networks to continuously learn new information without catastrophically forgetting what has been learnt before. Artificial neural networks are remarkably adept at sensory processing, sequence learning and reinforcement learning, but are limited in their ability to represent variables and data structures and to store data over long timescales, owing to the lack of an external memory. Here we introduce a machine learning model called a differentiable neural computer (DNC), which consists of a neural network that can read from and write to an external memory matrix, analogous to the random-access memory in a conventional computer. The interaction between short- and long-term memory is studied within a model in which phonemic and (temporal) contextual information have separate influences on immediate verbal serial recall via connections with short- and long-term plasticity [Burgess, N., & Hitch, G.J. Memory for serial order: a network model of the phonological loop and its timing. Humans regularly perform new learning without losing memory for previous information, but neural network models suffer from the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting in which new learning impairs prior function.

results.content: # Continual Learning and Catastrophic Forgetting. title={Continual Learning and Catastrophic Forgetting},. ### Addressing Catastrophic Forgetting and Beyond: Key Challenges in Continual Learning. This paper proposes a novel method for preventing catastrophic forgetting in machine learning applications, specifically focusing on neural networks by incorporating negotiated representations into the learning process, which allows the model to maintain a balance between retaining past experiences and adapting to new tasks. ### Continual Learning with Columnar Spiking Neural Networks. This study proposes columnar-organized spiking neural networks (SNNs) with local learning rules for continual learning and catastrophic forgetting, and demonstrates how CoLaNET hyperparameters govern the trade-off between retaining old knowledge and acquiring new information. ### Continual Learning in Convolutional Neural Networks with Tensor Rank Updates. A novel approach to CL in convolutional neural networks (CNN s) using tensor rank increments, which facilitates learning new tasks without forgetting previous ones, thereby achieving efficient learning. ### Continuous Learning for Children's ASR: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting with Elastic Weight Consolidation and Synaptic Intelligence. This paper presents, for the first time, a method for preventing catastrophic forgetting (BGD) for scenarios with task boundaries that are unknown during training --- task-agnostic continual learning. This paper finds that by equipping tabular and deep reinforcement learning agents with a synaptic model that incorporates this biological complexity, catastrophic forgetting can be mitigated at multiple timescales and can be used to overcome within-task forgetting by reducing the need for an experience replay database. A model for continual learning, called Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) is proposed that alleviates forgetting, while allowing beneficial transfer of knowledge to previous tasks. This work presents a new paradigm for continual learning that aims to train a more succinct memory system without accessing task identity at test time, and achieves competitive results against rehearsal-based methods even without a re-hearsal buffer. This work develops a generative classifier that efficiently uses data-driven experience to learn new concepts even from few samples while being immune to forgetting, suggesting that generative models provide a natural way for alleviating catastrophic forgetting, which is a major drawback of discriminative models.
